title: Taylor v. Caldwell
summary: The accidental destruction of the particular music hall essential to the planned concerts excused both sides from future performance.
notes: The agreement was made on May 27, 1861 for the Surrey Gardens and Music Hall on June 17, July 15, August 5 and August 19; the hall burned on June 11, 1861; Blackburn J.'s opinion (3 B. & S. 826, 122 Eng. Rep. 309) reads an implied condition that the parties are excused when performance becomes impossible through the perishing of the thing without fault of either side, the origin of the common-law impossibility/frustration doctrine.

sections.Parties: Taylor and the other plaintiffs organized concerts. Caldwell and the other defendants agreed to provide the Surrey Gardens and Music Hall and related entertainments.
sections.Material Facts:
The written arrangement gave the organizers use of the gardens and hall on four specified days for concerts and day-and-night festivities. The organizers were to pay £100 per day and receive admission receipts; the defendants would also supply a band and other amusements. The court construed the arrangement as use of the particular venue, rather than a lease.

Before the first concert, a fire destroyed the hall so completely that the entertainments could not take place as planned. Neither party was at fault. The agreement did not expressly allocate this casualty. The organizers had spent money advertising and preparing and sought those losses as damages for breach.
sections.Procedural History: A verdict was initially returned for the organizers with leave reserved to enter a verdict for the defendants. The Court of Queen's Bench (Blackburn J., 6 May 1863) directed entry of the defendants' verdict.
sections.Issue: Did the unqualified wording require compensation when the essential venue ceased to exist without either party’s fault?
sections.Holding: No. The parties’ performance depended on the continued existence of the particular hall; its fault-free destruction excused both sides.
sections.Reasoning:
Blackburn treated continued existence as an implied condition evident from the nature of the transaction. This was not simply a promise to provide any comparable entertainment space. The identified hall was the foundation of the performances the parties contemplated, and there was no warranty assuming the risk of its destruction.

The opinion developed the principle by analogy to personal services and the return of specific property. Its use of an implied condition explains how the court reconciled excuse with the general obligation to perform contractual promises. Later commentary in the assigned pages questions whether imaginary party intentions are the best justification; that criticism is distinct from the court’s own reasoning.

The ruling rejected the organizers’ breach claim for preparation expenses. It should not be read as an award reimbursing either side’s reliance or as an all-purpose answer to later restitution questions.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Taylor identifies a limited setting in which an unexpected event destroys an essential basis of performance, rather than merely making the promised work more costly.

topics.impracticability: Destruction of an essential, specific venue excused future performance.
topics.conditions: The court expressed excuse as an implied condition of continued existence.
topics.risk-allocation: No party had warranted against the hall’s fault-free destruction.
topics.reliance: Preparation expenses did not create a breach claim once performance was excused.
topics.frustration: Taylor v. Caldwell is the source of the English impossibility/frustration doctrine that Krell v. Henry later extended to frustration of purpose.
topics.gap-filling: Blackburn J. excused performance by reading in an implied condition of the hall's continued existence, an early example of a court supplying a term the parties did not write.

mnemonic.rationale: The music hall that burned down
